papers.title: A Comparative Study on Samskāra in the Yoga Sūtra and Nuclear Feeling in Tao-Psychotherapy: Focusing on the Restraint of Samskāra and the Dissolution of Nuclear Feeling
papers.abstract: This study aims to establish an integrated healing model by identifying the structural isomorphism between the concept of Samskāra in Patañjali’s Yoga Sūra and Nuclear Feeling in So-am Rhee Dong-shick’s Tao-Psychotherapy. First, the research demonstrates that Samskāra and Nuclear Feeling share seven functional similarities, particularly in terms of their formation period, located in prenatal stage, and their unconscious repetitive dynamics. By reinterpreting the metaphysical concept of the past as a prenatal origin within the present life, this study suggests that the two mechanisms can be understood as comparable forms of psychological imprinting. Second, the study argues that the ‘dissolution of nuclear feeling’ in Tao-Psychotherapy provides an essential condition for securing energetic plasticity, thereby enabling the yogic processes of the ‘restraint of Samskāa (nirodha)’ and ‘transformation (parināa).’Third, based on this comparison, the study proposes an ‘Integrated Model of Transformative Dissolution’ through which suffering may be transformed into a source of wisdom. By shifting the aim of healing from mere removal to transformation, this model explains how fixed emotional patterns can be reconstituted as positive existential resources ('Positive Transformation'). This study is significant in that it integrates ancient Eastern wisdom with a Korean psychotherapeutic model through the framework of prenatal experience, thereby offering practical implications for healing and clinical application.

papers.title: The effect of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy on sexual self-esteem in women with breast cancer after mastectomy: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Mastectomy often leads to decreased sexual self-esteem in women with breast cancer. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) on sexual self-esteem in women after mastectomy. METHODS: This randomized controlled trial (February-May 2024, Golestan Hospital, Ahvaz, Iran) enrolled 45 women aged 30-49 years after mastectomy. They were randomly assigned to an MBCT group (n = 22, eight weekly sessions) or a control group (n = 23, usual care). Sexual self-esteem was measured using the SSEI‑W‑SF at baseline and post-intervention. Data were analyzed using t‑tests and ANCOVA. RESULTS: No baseline differences were found between groups. Post-intervention, after controlling for confounders, the MBCT group showed significantly higher scores in total sexual self-esteem and subscales (attractiveness, experience/skills, control, adaptation) compared to controls (p < 0.001, η CONCLUSIONS: MBCT significantly improves sexual self-esteem and its components in women post-mastectomy. Integrating MBCT into survivorship care may address an overlooked aspect of breast cancer recovery. IMPLICATIONS FOR CANCER SURVIVORS: MBCT is an effective non-pharmacological intervention for improving sexual self-esteem in women after mastectomy, enhancing their quality of life. papers.title: The Effectiveness of Digital Intervention on Psychological Resilience in Postoperative Breast Cancer Patients During Chemotherapy Intervals: Quasi-Experimental Study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with breast cancer during postoperative chemotherapy intervals commonly experience psychological distress and reduced resilience while recovering at home. Digital mindfulness interventions may provide accessible psychological support during this vulnerable period; however, evidence regarding tailored interventions for postoperative patients with breast cancer during chemotherapy intervals remains limited. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to examine the effectiveness of a digital intervention on psychological resilience in postoperative patients with breast cancer during chemotherapy intervals. METHODS: A quasi-experimental study with repeated measures was conducted from October 2021 to June 2022. A total of 80 eligible participants were recruited from the Department of Breast Surgery at a tertiary hospital in Zhejiang Province, China, and 71 completed the study. The control group received routine discharge instructions and nursing follow-ups, whereas the intervention group additionally received an 8-week digital psychological resilience intervention. Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0), 3 months post intervention (T1), and 6 months post intervention (T2). The measures included the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Social Support Rating Scale (SSRS), Breast Cancer Survivor Self-Efficacy Scale (BCSSS), and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Breast (FACT-B). At T1, the intervention group had higher CD-RISC scores than the control group (mean 67.58, SD 11.41 vs mean 62.09, SD 10.18;  CONCLUSIONS: The digital psychological resilience intervention effectively alleviated anxiety and depression in postoperative patients with breast cancer during chemotherapy intervals. It also significantly enhanced their psychological resilience and self-efficacy in the early postintervention phase. Although the improvements in psychological resilience and self-efficacy did not remain statistically superior to those of the control group at the 6-month endpoint, the intervention improved the recovery trajectory of the patients and provided significant short-term benefits during the early postintervention period. Future research should explore strategies to maintain these gains over the long term.

papers.title: Incorporating a Mindfulness-Based Mental Health Intervention on Short-Term Mission Trips.
papers.abstract: In Honduras, a lack of mental health providers and the difficult terrain limit access to mental health care. During a week-long healthcare mission clinic, nurse practitioners provided Scriptures and a 5-minute mindfulness-based stress reduction intervention to participants who had scored 5 or above (suggesting moderate to high stress) on the Stress Visual Numeric Scale. Spontaneous patient feedback indicated the intervention was helpful. The descriptive survey findings indicate high self-reported stress levels among participants and that stress screening and intervention can be implemented efficiently within a healthcare mission clinic setting.

papers.title: Communication barriers for d/Deaf people with cancer: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Significant healthcare disparities can be experienced by d/Deaf individuals, particularly in accessing effective communication and health information. Limited research has examined the experiences of d/Deaf cancer patients or how their interactions with healthcare professionals (HCPs) and communication support professionals (CSPs) influence their quality of care. This scoping review aimed to map current evidence about the communication and unmet needs of d/Deaf cancer patients, educational needs of HCPs and roles of CSPs. METHODS: Following the Joanna Briggs Institute method for Scoping Reviews, database searches were conducted on PsycInfo, PubMed, Embase, CINAHL and Scopus, and grey literature was identified. Papers published in English that reported on the experiences of d/Deaf cancer patients and their communication with HCPs and CSPs were included. Thematic analysis was used to identify key descriptive themes. RESULTS: Only nine (1 quantitative, 7 qualitative, 1 mixed-methods) papers were included. Most focused on d/Deaf cancer patients (mainly breast cancer); only 1 included HCPs and none examined CSPs. Three main themes and 9 subthemes were identified that negatively impacted d/Deaf cancer patients' views about their healthcare: system-level factors; interpersonal factors and patient-level factors. The HCP-focused paper highlighted that collaboration with interpreting services enhanced communication and patient understanding. CONCLUSIONS: Despite limited data, this review highlights multiple barriers d/Deaf patients can encounter when accessing cancer services. Collectively, these may affect effective communication practices and can compromise the quality of care delivered. Data supports accessible educational resources, improved access to qualified medical interpreters and deaf awareness training for HCPs.
